strengths: Addresses a practically important bottleneck in vision-language reranking and presents a coherent two-stage retrieval design that moves visual encoding offline.
The proposed system offers an appealing efficiency profile: a compact MiniLM joint encoder and compressed visual tokens substantially reduce online latency, storage, and parameter count.
Experiments cover several vision-backbone families, and EDJE consistently improves the corresponding embedding-only retrieval results on Flickr30K.
The paper includes useful ablations on token count, reranking-pool size, auxiliary objectives, and distillation, and it is generally clear and well organized.
weaknesses: The architectural novelty is limited. Caching vision features, projecting them into a language model, and compressing them using learned cross-attention queries closely resemble established VLM adapters, Perceiver-style resamplers, and Q-Former mechanisms; the paper primarily combines known components.

The central large-scale claim is not validated on a large-scale retrieval corpus. Evaluation is restricted to Flickr30K and COCO, with no million-scale index, measured disk-I/O cost, end-to-end query latency, memory analysis, or first-stage retrieval cost.

Comparisons with prior joint encoders are substantially confounded: EDJE uses the much newer SigLIP2 backbone, whereas ALBEF/BLIP baselines use their original older backbones. Thus, the results do not isolate the benefit of EDJE's joint-encoder design.

Efficiency accounting is insufficiently controlled. Feature precision and implementation details for storage and latency comparisons are not specified consistently across methods, and the reported 1.91 ms for a batch of 64 corresponds to roughly 33.5k pairs/second rather than the abstract's stated 50k pairs/second.

The evaluation lacks strong contemporary efficient-reranker baselines and simple controls, such as an equivalently sized cross-attention encoder, alternative pooling/resampling adapters, or parameter- and backbone-matched baselines.

Reproducibility is incomplete: code and checkpoints are only promised, while important training details such as phase durations, loss weights, training batch size, compute budget, and complete sampling procedure are absent. The appendix also labels the third objective as ITC, whereas the main text describes text-embedding recovery, and lists 'Hard negatives: None' despite the stated hard-negative mining procedure.

Results are reported from apparently single runs without uncertainty, and the ablations mostly use only Flickr30K R@1. Broader datasets, robustness tests, and statistical variation are needed to establish that the modest gains over strong embedding models generalize.

strengths: The paper identifies a relevant systems problem and presents a clear offline/online decomposition: visual extraction and token compression are performed once, while a compact MiniLM-based joint encoder handles online reranking.
The same-backbone experiments show consistent Recall@1 gains over CLIP, DFN, MetaCLIP, and SigLIP2 retrieval, indicating that joint reranking provides value beyond stronger initial embeddings.

The evaluation reports several useful efficiency dimensions—latency, storage, and parameter count—and includes ablations on compression level, reranking-pool size, training objectives, and distillation.
The method is technically plausible, clearly described, and tested with multiple vision-backbone families.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is limited. Offline feature caching, learnable-query token compression, projection into a language model, and joint reranking closely resemble established ideas from cached late-interaction systems, attention pooling, Perceiver-style resampling, and Q-Former-based models. The contribution is primarily a useful engineering combination rather than a substantial methodological advance.

The central claim of practical large-scale retrieval is not convincingly evaluated. Experiments use only Flickr30K and COCO, with Flickr evaluation containing 1,000 images; there is no million-scale corpus, end-to-end retrieval benchmark, disk-I/O measurement, cache-loading analysis, index-update cost, or accounting of offline preprocessing. Even 49 kB per image corresponds to roughly 49 TB for one billion images.

The prior-art comparison is substantially confounded by backbone quality and pretraining. EDJE uses the much newer SigLIP2 backbone, while ALBEF/BLIP baselines use their original older encoders. The listed “training data” also omits the potentially enormous pretraining data used to obtain SigLIP2, so it does not establish a controlled comparison of the proposed architecture.

The storage comparison appears inconsistent in numerical precision: the reported ALBEF/BLIP cache sizes match FP32 token storage, whereas EDJE's 442 kB local cache matches 576×384 FP16 values. Without a common datatype and detailed accounting, the claimed storage advantage is overstated.

The headline throughput claim is internally inconsistent. Table 2 reports 1.91 ms for a batch of 64, which corresponds to about 33.5k pairs/s, not the abstract's 50k pairs/s. The appendix separately states an evaluation batch size of 32, adding further ambiguity. Latency methodology, synchronization, warmup, precision, and data-transfer inclusion are unspecified.

The default reranking pool is only k=10, despite motivating scenarios with thousands of candidates. This caps final recall by first-stage recall and makes Recall@5/10 gains mostly negligible. The larger-pool ablation reports accuracy but not the associated latency, throughput, or memory, leaving the important quality–cost tradeoff unresolved.

Reproducibility and diagnostic evidence are insufficient: checkpoints are only promised for future release; training epochs/steps, loss weights, compute, seeds, and variance are missing. Ablations report a single ambiguous R@1 value, the appendix labels text-embedding recovery as “ITC” even though Section 4 defines a different objective, and “Hard negatives: None” conflicts with the described in-batch hard-negative mining. Overall, these issues make the work technically plausible but not competitive for acceptance in its current form. strengths: The paper identifies a practically important bottleneck in vision-language reranking and presents a coherent systems solution: precompute visual features, compress them with learned queries, and perform online interaction using a compact joint encoder.

The accuracy-efficiency tradeoff is compelling. The 64-token model obtains Flickr30k zero-shot R@1 of 86.9/96.4 and COCO fine-tuned R@1 of 64.6/80.9 while using 49 kB per image, 33M online parameters, and a reported 1.91 ms per batch of 64—close to substantially larger BLIP-family models at much lower online cost.
Experiments cover several embedding backbones and show consistent reranking improvements, supporting the claim that EDJE is modular rather than tied to one vision encoder.

The paper includes useful ablations on token count, reranking-pool size, auxiliary objectives, and distillation. In particular, the compression and distillation results quantify meaningful design tradeoffs.
The presentation is clear, the architecture is easy to understand, and the work addresses a gap with direct relevance to practical multimodal retrieval systems.
weaknesses: The main architectural ingredients are individually familiar: cached vision features, learned-query compression closely related to Q-Former/attention pooling, and concatenation into a small Transformer. The novelty lies primarily in their retrieval-oriented combination and empirical characterization rather than a fundamentally new method.

The evaluation is narrow for the paper’s large-scale and practical-deployment claims: it uses only Flickr30k and COCO, with no genuinely large corpus, out-of-domain benchmark, hard compositional retrieval dataset, or production-style workload.

The efficiency evaluation isolates joint-encoder computation under a cached-vision regime but does not measure disk I/O, host-to-device transfer, end-to-end query latency, index construction, or offline encoding/compression cost. These omitted costs are central when cached tokens are the proposed scalability mechanism.

Most headline results use a reranking pool of only 10. Although pool-size robustness is plotted up to roughly 140, the paper does not report the corresponding latency, throughput, and data-transfer costs or evaluate the hundreds-to-thousands of candidates common in demanding reranking settings.

The reported 50k pairs/second claim is not transparently reconciled with Table 2: 64 samples in 1.91 ms corresponds to roughly 33.5k pairs/second. The appendix also lists evaluation batch size 32 whereas Table 2 states batch size 64.

Reproducibility remains incomplete: code and checkpoints are only promised, and important training details such as phase durations, loss weights, compute budget, and seed variability are missing. No confidence intervals or repeated-run results are reported.

The auxiliary-objective description is inconsistent: the main text describes text-embedding recovery, whereas the appendix labels the corresponding component ITC and calls it contrastive learning. This should be clarified.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important bottleneck in vision-language retrieval and presents a coherent architecture: expensive visual processing and token compression occur offline, while a compact MiniLM joint encoder performs online re-ranking. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/e7cd7820667a4dd18bb649ec91b01814/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

EDJE consistently improves Recall@1 over its underlying embedding retrievers across CLIP, DFN, MetaCLIP, and SigLIP2 backbones. The compressed SigLIP2 variant is competitive with prior joint encoders despite using substantially less training data and a smaller online model.

The paper considers accuracy, latency, and storage jointly. The 64-token representation retains most of the uncompressed model's accuracy while reducing storage from 442 kB to 49 kB per image, and the appendix additionally measures SSD-access costs.

The empirical analysis is broader than the main tables alone: it studies token count, pool size, training objectives, distillation, cross-model negative mining, alternative compression methods, quantization, and text-encoder choice. Learned compression consistently outperforms striding, clustering, and attention pruning.
weaknesses: The architectural novelty is moderate. Offline feature caching, learnable-query cross-attention compression, and projected visual tokens consumed by a language transformer closely resemble established ideas from retrieval systems, Perceiver-style pooling, Q-Former, and multimodal LLM adapters. The contribution is primarily a useful engineering combination rather than a clearly new modeling principle.

The principal comparison in Table 2 is not sufficiently controlled. EDJE uses the much newer SigLIP2 backbone, whereas ALBEF, BLIP, and BLIP-2 use different vision encoders, data scales, feature dimensions, numerical precisions, and fusion architectures. The reported storage comparison appears especially confounded: prior methods' large FP32 backbone features are compared against EDJE's lower-dimensional BF16 representations. Stronger controlled baselines using the same vision backbone and precision are needed.

The large-scale efficiency claim is not convincingly demonstrated end to end. The main experiments re-rank only k=10 candidates, while the headline throughput is based on isolated GPU joint-encoding latency. Candidate retrieval, random token fetches, host-to-device transfer, dequantization, batching, and concurrent-query behavior are not included in a unified benchmark. Moreover, 1.91 ms for a batch of 64 in Table 2 corresponds to about 33.5k rather than 50k pairs/second, leaving the headline number insufficiently explained.

Evaluation is confined largely to Flickr30k and COCO, both relatively small and saturated caption-retrieval benchmarks. The full-dataset experiment compares only against the older LightningDOT system. Results on genuinely large collections and challenging compositional, long-tail, or out-of-domain retrieval benchmarks would be important for substantiating robustness and practical impact.

Reproducibility details are incomplete despite the claimed public code release: the displayed code URL is empty, and the appendix omits training duration or step counts, training batch size, loss weights, optimizer betas, data preprocessing and deduplication details, compute budget, and random seeds. No uncertainty estimates or repeated-run results are reported for retrieval accuracy.

There are methodological inconsistencies that impede interpretation. The main text describes a text-embedding recovery objective, while Appendix B labels it ITC or text-image contrastive learning; the exact combined objective and its weighting are unspecified. The interpretability analysis is also weak evidence because nearest-neighbor vocabulary projections and the alignment statistic are closely tied to the model's learned projection space.

The manuscript does not discuss biases, licensing, or privacy issues associated with its web-sourced pretraining datasets, despite motivating deployment in applications such as web search, dataset curation, and content moderation. Overall, the system is promising and technically plausible, but the novelty, comparison fairness, reproducibility, and end-to-end evidence fall slightly below the acceptance threshold.

strengths: The paper targets a practically relevant problem: reducing the online cost and storage footprint of vision-language re-ranking by caching visual features and using a small joint encoder.
The architecture is clearly motivated, and the separation between offline visual processing and online joint encoding is easy to understand and potentially useful in retrieval systems.
EDJE improves Recall@1 over the corresponding embedding retriever across several backbone families, including the relatively strong SigLIP2 model.

The paper includes useful studies of token count, training objectives, distillation, negative mining, quantization, text-encoder choice, and alternative compression strategies. The learned compression module consistently outperforms the tested striding, clustering, and attention-pruning baselines.

Reporting latency, representation storage, I/O measurements, and full-dataset retrieval goes beyond an accuracy-only evaluation. weaknesses: The technical novelty is limited. Precomputing visual features, projecting them into a language model, and compressing them with learned cross-attention queries closely resemble established cached-feature retrieval, Perceiver-style resampling, and Q-Former mechanisms. The paper primarily combines known components rather than introducing a substantially new modeling principle.

The central comparison to prior joint encoders is heavily confounded. EDJE uses the much newer SigLIP2 visual representation, whereas ALBEF and BLIP use older backbones. Counting only EDJE's 12M task-training pairs also ignores the potentially much larger pretraining investment behind SigLIP2. Consequently, Table 2 does not isolate the contribution of the proposed joint encoder or compression method.

The claimed 50k-pairs/second throughput is not supported by the reported measurements. Table 2 reports 1.91 ms for a batch of 64, which corresponds to roughly 33.5k pairs/second, and no separate experiment explaining the 50k figure is provided. End-to-end throughput, including candidate lookup, random token reads, transfer, and scoring, is not measured.

The large-scale deployment claim is insufficiently validated. Most experiments re-rank only the top 10 candidates on small, saturated Flickr30K and COCO benchmarks. The appendix's 50k-candidate I/O benchmark is disconnected from the default retrieval pipeline and uses a 100k-image local index; it is not an end-to-end evaluation at million- or billion-image scale. At 49 kB per image, a billion-image index would still require about 49 TB.

The empirical scope is narrow for claims about fine-grained joint modeling. Evaluation is restricted to conventional caption retrieval, with no compositional, relation-sensitive, long-text, multilingual, or hard-negative retrieval benchmarks where cross-modal joint interaction should provide its clearest advantage.

Reported improvements lack uncertainty estimates, repeated runs, or significance analysis. This matters because several gains over strong retrievers and differences among compression settings are small on highly saturated test sets.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The hyperparameter appendix omits training duration or step counts, loss weights, data sampling proportions, preprocessing and augmentation details, and several implementation choices needed to reproduce latency. It also contains inconsistencies: Section 4 describes text-embedding recovery, whereas Table 4 calls the objective image-text contrastive learning; Table 3 states 'Hard negatives: None' despite the method relying on in-batch hard-negative selection.

The interpretability analysis does not substantiate the strong semantic conclusions. Nearest-neighbor vocabulary projections can produce plausible words without demonstrating grounded token semantics, only two qualitative examples are shown, and the comparison is affected by the compressed representation being explicitly trained in the language embedding space. The Figure 9 caption also says compression shifts scores lower, while the accompanying numerical results say its mean is higher.

Some efficiency comparisons are underspecified, including precision, compilation and kernel settings, data-transfer treatment, warm-up, number of timing repetitions, and whether competing implementations received comparable optimization. This prevents the headline speedup from being assessed reliably.

Overall, the paper contains a sensible engineering direction and encouraging results, but the incremental novelty, confounded comparisons, unsupported throughput claim, and limited end-to-end scaling evidence leave the principal claims below the standard for acceptance at a top-tier AI conference.

strengths: The paper addresses a clear and practically important bottleneck in vision-language retrieval: making cross-modal re-ranking feasible when image features can be computed offline.
EDJE is simple, modular, and effective. Across several embedding-model families, re-ranking consistently improves Recall@1, including meaningful gains over the strong SigLIP2 retriever.

The reported accuracy-efficiency trade-off is compelling: the compressed model remains close to prior joint encoders while using a 33M-parameter online encoder, substantially lower latency, and only 49 kB of cached features per image.

The evaluation includes useful ablations of token count, training objectives, distillation, negative mining, re-ranking depth, alternative compression methods, quantization, and text-encoder choice. The learned compression adapter consistently outperforms generic pruning, striding, and clustering baselines.
The deployment discussion, I/O measurements, full-dataset experiments, and indexing/retrieval pseudocode make the practical contribution more concrete than a purely benchmark-oriented study.
The manuscript is generally clear and well organized, and the main empirical conclusions are easy to follow.
weaknesses: The architectural novelty is moderate. Offline feature caching, learned-query token compression, modality projection, and joint processing by a language transformer closely resemble established Q-Former/Perceiver-resampler and VLM design patterns; the main contribution is their effective systems-oriented combination.

The comparison with prior joint encoders is substantially confounded. EDJE uses a modern SigLIP2 backbone whereas ALBEF and BLIP use older vision encoders, and the table's training-data column omits the potentially very large pretraining cost and data of the frozen backbones. A controlled comparison using the same vision features would better isolate EDJE's contribution.

Evaluation is concentrated on Flickr30k and COCO, which are relatively small and saturated benchmarks. There is no evaluation on modern compositional, hard-negative, domain-shift, or genuinely web-scale retrieval benchmarks, while the only full-dataset baseline is the older LightningDOT method.

The headline throughput claim is insufficiently substantiated and appears inconsistent with Table 2: 1.91 ms for a batch of 64 corresponds to roughly 33.5k rather than 50k pairs per second. Reported online latency also excludes first-stage retrieval and apparently excludes storage access and dequantization. The appendix measures I/O separately, but does not provide end-to-end query latency or throughput.

The storage cost remains significant at true web scale: 49 kB per image is about 49 TB per billion images before indexing and replication. This should be contextualized against compressed source images and standard embedding indexes rather than described simply as practical at scale.

Reproducibility details remain incomplete despite the hyperparameter appendix: training duration or step counts, loss weights, dataset sampling, hardware cost, random seeds, and uncertainty across runs are absent. There are also terminology inconsistencies between text-embedding recovery and 'ITC,' and the table states 'Hard negatives: None' despite the described in-batch hard-negative procedure.
